newsitem.title: UK: UK rate rise still on cards despite good Dec RPIs.
newsitem.headline: UK rate rise still on cards despite good Dec RPIs.

text.p: A dip in both headline and underlying UK inflation in December justifies the Chancellor's decision to keep interest rates on hold, economists said, but rates will probably still have to rise in February if price pressures are to remain in check.
Inflation is expected to continue edging down in 1997, although the government's ambitious target for an underlying rate of 2.5 percent remains out of reach for the medium term.
"These were excellent numbers," said HSBC Markets economist Jonathan Loynes of the dip in underlying inflation to 3.1 pct.
"They are the first sign that the sharp fall in factory gate inflation over the last year is finally feeding into the retail environment."

Official data showed headline inflation rose 0.3 percent in December to an annual rate of 2.5 percent, down from 2.7 percent in November. The underlying rate fell to 3.1 percent from 3.3 percent, at which it had been stuck for the last two months.

Economists said while it was possible Chancellor Kenneth Clarke would order a rise in interest rates at the next monetary meeting on February 5, he may yet succumb to political pressure and try to tough it out until after the election.
"I suspect he will concede another rate rise in February provided the GDP and monthly data point towards an accelerating economy," said Schroders economist David Philpotts.
"I don't think there would be any electoral downside if he concedes another quarter percent."
Union Plc chief economist Philip Shaw said the fourth quarter GDP data due on January 27 would be crucial.
"If it shows above trend growth in the economy, the Bank of England will be very concerned about the longer term outlook for UK inflation," he said.

"And with the Bank's inflation report coming out a week or so after the monetary meeting in February, I don't think the Chancellor will want a showdown on the economy with the Bank so close to the election."
With the trend rate of UK economic growth at around 2.5 percent, a quarterly rise in Q4 GDP above 0.6 percent would start to ring alarm bells for the Bank on inflation, Shaw said.
Economists said December's fall in inflation would likely herald the start of easing price pressures in 1997.

"With the strength of the pound likely to keep costs under tight control this year, while wage pressures remain subdued, we expect underlying inflation to fall sharply, ending the year within the government's target range of 2.5 percent or less," said Loynes.
But Schroder's Philpotts was more pessimistic.

"The government has never really been on course for its target (by the end of the parliament) and it won't be at least until beyond 1998," he said, adding 2.5 percent was an unfeasibly low target for an economy at the top of its economic cycle.
Shaw was also slightly more cautious. "It's touch and go for meeting it by the end of this year," he said. "But we're looking for underlying inflation to edge down over the next few months."
But he said factors such as rising council taxes in April may disrupt inflation's downward path.
Economists said lower-than-expected rises in seasonal food and house prices accounted for part of the fall in inflation.

"The RPI was assisted by weak food prices...helped by the strength of sterling," said General Accident economist Andrew Milligan. "This should be the short term peak in RPIX unless oil prices show a further surge."
